2007B16.goal: $10\%$ juniors (all with the same score $J$), $90\%$ seniors averaging $83$, overall average $84$. We want $J$. The overall average is a weighted average.

tools.name: Weighted average
tools.why: Each group's average is weighted by its share.

2007B16.shortcut: Seniors are $1$ point below average with weight $9$; juniors must be $9$ points above: $84+9=93$.
2007B16.recognize: Mixtures of groups: balance the deviations from the overall mean.

2007B17.goal: $P$ is inside equilateral $\triangle ABC$ with perpendicular distances $1,2,3$ to the sides. We want $AB$. The three distances add up to the altitude.

tools.name: Viviani's theorem
tools.why: Split $\triangle ABC$ into three triangles from $P$: $\tfrac12s(d_1+d_2+d_3)=\tfrac12sh$.

tools.name: Equilateral altitude
tools.why: 30-60-90 triangle.

2007B17.bridge: Sum the distances to get the altitude.
2007B17.shortcut: Viviani: for any interior point, the distance sum is constant.
2007B17.recognize: Distances from an interior point to the sides of an equilateral triangle: they sum to the altitude.

2007B18.goal: A unit circle is surrounded by $4$ circles of radius $r$, each tangent to it and to its two neighbours. We want $r$. The outer centres form a square.

tools.name: Square of centres
tools.why: Neighbouring outer circles touch.

tools.name: Tangency to the middle
tools.why: The middle-to-outer centre distance is $1+r$.

steps.title: Equation
steps.explain: Distance from the middle to an outer centre: $r\sqrt2$ (half-diagonal) $=1+r$.

check.q: A square with side $2r$ has half-diagonal?

solution: Outer centres form a square of side $2r$.
2007B18.shortcut: Right isosceles triangle on two outer centres and the middle: legs $1+r$, hypotenuse $2r$.
2007B18.recognize: Ring of equal circles around a centre circle: regular polygon of centres.

2007B19.goal: A wheel with six equal sectors ($1,2,3,6,7,9$) is spun twice. The first number mod $4$ picks a column, the second mod $5$ a row, on a checkerboard. We want $P(\text{shaded})$. On a checkerboard, shading depends only on parities.

tools.name: Checkerboard parity
tools.why: Colours alternate in both directions.

tools.name: A fair parity forces 1/2
tools.why: Whatever the column, exactly one row parity shades it.

2007B19.approach: Rows: $1,2,3,6,7,9\bmod5=1,2,3,1,2,4$ — odd ($1,3,1$) exactly half the time. Independent of the column, the shaded parity occurs with probability $\tfrac12$.

steps.title: Row parity
steps.explain: Row remainders $1,2,3,1,2,4$: three odd, three even.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.explain: For any fixed column, the shaded squares in it are exactly the rows of one parity, which has probability $\tfrac12$. So $P=\tfrac12$.

check.q: If the row parity is a fair coin independent of the column, what is $P(\text{shaded})$?

solution: Row remainders: $1,2,3,1,2,4$, odd half the time.
On a checkerboard, each column's shaded rows form one parity class.
2007B19.shortcut: You never need the column distribution once the row parity is fair.
traps: Counting shaded squares and dividing by the board size.
2007B19.recognize: Random squares on a checkerboard: look for a coordinate whose parity is exactly $50/50$.

2007B20.goal: Choose $3$ of the $25$ blocks in a $5\times5$ square with no two in the same row or column. Pick the rows, the columns, then match them.

tools.name: Choose rows and columns
tools.why: Three distinct rows and three distinct columns.

tools.name: Matching
tools.why: Pair each chosen row with a different chosen column.

steps.title: Match
steps.explain: $3!=6$ ways to pair rows with columns. Total $600$.

2007B20.recognize: Non-attacking rooks: choose rows, choose columns, permute.

2007B21.goal: A square $XYZW$ sits with $XY$ on the hypotenuse $AC$ of a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle and its top corners on the legs. We want its side $s$. Use the altitude to the hypotenuse and similar triangles.

tools.name: Altitude to hypotenuse
tools.why: Twice the area over the hypotenuse.

tools.name: Similar top triangle
tools.why: $WZ\parallel AC$, so the triangle above the square is similar to $ABC$.

2007B21.approach: The triangle $WBZ$ above the square has base $s$ and height $h-s$, similar to $ABC$ (base $5$, height $h$). So $s=\tfrac{5h}{5+h}$.
traps: Using the square in the right-angle corner ($\tfrac{12}7$).
2007B21.recognize: Square inscribed with a side on a triangle's base: $s=\tfrac{bh}{b+h}$.

2007B22.goal: Two tetrahedral dice; the player wins $1$ if their number appears once, $2$ if twice, loses $1$ if not at all. We want the expected return.

tools.name: Binomial probabilities
tools.why: Each die shows the number with probability $\tfrac14$.

tools.name: Expected value
tools.why: Weighted average of outcomes.

check.q: What is $P(\text{exactly one die shows it})$?

2007B22.bridge: Weight each payoff by its probability.
2007B22.shortcut: Over $16$ equally likely outcomes, total winnings $2+6-9=-1$.
2007B22.recognize: Simple games: list outcomes, multiply payoffs by probabilities.

2007B23.goal: A plane parallel to the base, $2$ above it, cuts off a top pyramid with half the original surface area. We want the original height $h$. The top pyramid is similar to the original.

tools.name: Area scaling
tools.why: Similar solids with length ratio $k$.

tools.name: Heights
tools.why: The top pyramid's height is $k$ times the original's.

check.q: If similar solids have area ratio $\tfrac12$, what is the length ratio?
check.why: Square root of the area ratio.

2007B23.bridge: Scale factor from area, then heights.
2007B23.recognize: Cutting parallel to the base: similar solids; areas scale by $k^2$, volumes by $k^3$.

2007B24.goal: We want the smallest number using only $4$s and $9$s (at least one each) divisible by $4$ and $9$, and its last four digits.

tools.name: Divisible by 4
tools.why: Of $44,49,94,99$ only $44$ is a multiple of $4$.

tools.name: Divisible by 9
tools.why: $a$ = number of $4$s.

2007B24.approach: Need nine $4$s (fewest), at least one $9$, ending in $44$. Smallest: $10$ digits with the $9$ as far right as allowed: $4444444944$.

steps.title: Counts
steps.explain: Nine $4$s and one $9$ is the shortest possibility ($10$ digits).

check.q: How many $4$s are needed for divisibility by $9$?

steps.title: Arrange
steps.explain: The last two digits are $44$, so the $9$ goes in the third-to-last place: $4444444944$. Last four digits $4944$.

check.q: Where should the single $9$ go for the smallest number?
check.why: Big digits belong in low places.

2007B24.bridge: Fix the ending, count the $4$s, push the $9$ right.
solution: Ends in $44$; number of $4$s is a multiple of $9$.
2007B24.shortcut: Using nine $9$s instead would be longer; nine $4$s plus one $9$ is minimal.
2007B24.recognize: Restricted-digit multiples: handle each divisibility rule separately, then minimise.

2007B25.goal: Count coprime $(a,b)$ with $\tfrac ab+\tfrac{14b}{9a}=\tfrac{9a^2+14b^2}{9ab}$ an integer. Use divisibility by $a$, by $b$ and by $9$.

tools.name: Divisibility by 9
tools.why: $9a^2$ is already divisible by $9$.

check.why: The numerator must be divisible by $9$.

2007B25.bridge: Bound $a$ and $b$ by divisibility, then test.
2007B25.shortcut: With $b=9$, $a^2+126\equiv a^2\pmod9$ needs $3\mid a$, impossible for $a\mid14$.
2007B25.recognize: Fractions that must be integers with coprime variables: each variable divides the "other" term.
